title: The Roll Call of Faith (Hebrews 11)
lead: Hebrews 11 retells Israel's story, from Abel to the Maccabean martyrs, as a line of people who trusted God's word about things not yet seen; Hebrews 12:1 then calls them 'a cloud of witnesses' around the church. Other passages also review the ancestors to teach the present generation: Psalm 78, Psalm 105, Psalm 106, Nehemiah 9, Stephen's speech in Acts 7, and outside the 66 books Sirach 44-50 and 1 Maccabees 2:51-60.

sections.b: Israel's Scriptures often teach by retelling the past. Psalm 78 recites the exodus and the wilderness so that the next generation "would set their confidence in God" (Psalm 78:7) and not be like their fathers; Psalms 105 and 106 tell the same story as God's faithfulness and Israel's failure; Nehemiah 9 is a prayer of confession that walks from creation to the return from exile. Stephen's speech (Acts 7) reviews Abraham, Joseph and Moses to show a people who resisted God's messengers. Outside the Hebrew Bible, Sirach praises the ancestors in chapters 44-50, the Wisdom of Solomon (chapter 10) retells the story from Adam to the exodus as the work of Wisdom saving the righteous, and the dying Mattathias tells his sons, "Remember the deeds our ancestors did in their generations" (1 Maccabees 2:51). Hebrews 11 stands in this line, with one difference: it chooses its examples for a single quality, faith, and ends not with the ancestors but with the hearers.
sections.refs: Psalm 78:1-8; Psalm 105; Psalm 106; Nehemiah 9:6-37; Acts 7:2-53; 1 Maccabees 2:51-64; Hebrews 11:1-40; Wisdom of Solomon 10:1-21

sections.h: The order of the roll call
sections.b: Hebrews follows Scripture's order: before the flood (Abel, Enoch, Noah), the patriarchs (Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph), the exodus (Moses' parents, Moses, the Passover, the sea), the conquest (Jericho, Rahab), then a quick list (Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, the prophets) and a list of deeds and sufferings without names, which readers connect with Daniel, Elijah and Elisha, the Maccabean martyrs and the prophets killed by kings. The repeated 'by faith' and the frame 'given a good witness' (Hebrews 11:2, 39) hold it together.
sections.refs: Hebrews 11:2-40; Genesis 4-50; Exodus 1-15; Joshua 2-6; Judges 4-16; 1 Samuel 1-17

sections.b: 4 Maccabees, a Jewish book in Greek (outside the Jewish, Catholic and Protestant Bibles), puts a short roll call in the mouth of the mother of the seven martyrs. In the Greek text as Swete prints it, she reminds her sons that Abraham hurried to sacrifice Isaac, that Daniel was thrown to the lions, and that Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael were thrown into the furnace and 'endured for God's sake', and then tells them that they have 'the same faith toward God' (4 Maccabees 16:20-22). Like Hebrews 11, it joins Abraham's offering, the lions and the fire, and calls the hearers to endure with the same faith.

sections.h: 'A cloud of witnesses' and the saints (Hebrews 12:1)
sections.b: Hebrews 12:1 calls the people of chapter 11 'so huge a cloud of witnesses surrounding us'. Churches draw different things from the verse. The Catholic Catechism cites it under the heading 'A cloud of witnesses': 'The witnesses who have preceded us into the kingdom, especially those whom the Church recognizes as saints, share in the living tradition of prayer', and 'We can and should ask them to intercede for us and for the whole world' (paragraph 2683). The Lutheran Augsburg Confession teaches 'that the memory of saints may be set before us, that we may follow their faith and good works', but says that 'the Scripture teaches not the invocation of saints or to ask help of saints, since it sets before us the one Christ as the Mediator' (article 21). Readers on both sides agree that the verse holds up the faithful dead as examples; they divide over whether the living may ask for their prayers.
